blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Oxidation number (or oxidation state) of an atom in a molecule or ion is the hypothetical or real charge present on an atom due to electronegativity difference.

Or

Oxidation number (or oxidation state) of an element in a compound represents the number of electrons lost or gained during its change from free state into that compound.

Some important points about oxidation number :

• Electronegativity values of no two elements are same.
    • Oxidation number of an element may be positive or negative.
    • Oxidation number can be zero, whole number or a fractional value.
    • Oxidation number of same element can be different in same or different compounds.

blocks.title: Oxidation Number
blocks.text:
Some Helping Rules for Calculating Oxidation Number:

In case of covalent bond:

• The oxidation number of an element in homoatomic molecules / free state / allotropic / alloy / Ligand are zero.
    • Oxidation number of fluorine in all its compounds is –1.
    • Oxidation number of IA & II A group elements are +1 and +2 respectively.
    • Oxidation number of hydrogen in most of its compounds is +1 except in metal hydrides (-1).
    • Oxidation number of oxygen in most of its compounds is -2.
    • Oxidation number of monoatomic ions is equal to the charge present on the ion.
    • The algebraic sum of oxidation number of all the atoms present in a polyatomic neutral molecule is 0.
    • The algebraic sum of oxidation number of all the atoms in a polyatomic ion is equal to the charge present on the ion.

In case of co-ordinate bond: (+ 2 → ー2)

In case of Ionic bond: Charge on cation = O.N of cation, Charge on anion = O.N of anion

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question: Oxidation number of cobalt in $[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_2Br$ is-
blocks.answer:
Let the oxidation number of Co be x

NH3 is a neutral ligand so O.N. is 0

Oxidation number of Cl is –1

Oxidation number of Br is –1

Hence, x + 6 (0) – (1 × 2) – 1 = 0

∵ x = + 3

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.question:
The oxidation number of S in $\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_8$ is –

(1) +8

(2) –8

(3) +6

(4) +4
blocks.answer:
In H2S2O8 , two O atoms form peroxide linkage i.e.

2 × 1 + 2x + 6 (–2) + 2 (–1) = 0

x = + 6

Thus the oxidation number of S in H2S2O8 is + 6

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Not Following the Basic Rules of Oxidation Numbers.
  • Forgetting the Oxidation Number of Hydrogen and Oxygen.
  • Misassigning Oxidation Numbers in Polyatomic Ions.
  • Ignoring the Sum of Oxidation Numbers in Neutral Compounds.
  • Overlooking Exceptions.
Note :

To avoid these common mistakes, always:

  • Start by applying the basic rules in order, considering the element's position in the periodic table and its usual bonding behaviour.
  • Check the sum of oxidation states in neutral compounds and polyatomic ions.
  • Apply exceptions and special rules, particularly for oxygen, hydrogen, and transition metals.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Redox Reaction:

A reaction in which oxidation and reduction simultaneously take place.

In all redox reactions the total increase in oxidation number must equal the total decrease in oxidation number.

Oxidising and Reducing Nature of the Substances:

• Oxidising agents / Oxidising power / Oxidant : (gain electrons)

Oxidising agents are those compounds which can oxidise others and reduced itself during the

chemical reaction.

• Reducing agents / Reducing power / Reductant : (loses electrons)
Reducing agents are those compound which can reduce others and oxidise itself during the

chemical reaction.

Types of Redox Reactions:

• Intermolecular redox reaction :- When oxidation and reduction takes place separately in different compounds.
    • Intramolecular redox reaction :- When reduction and oxidation takes place in the different elements of the same compound.
    • Disproportionation redox reaction :- When reduction and oxidation takes place in the same element of the same compound.
    • Comproportionation redox  reaction :- Reverse of disproportionation reaction.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question:
H2O2 + H2O2 → 2H2O + O2 is an example of disproportionation because -

(1) Oxidation number of oxygen only decreases

(2) Oxidation number of oxygen only increases

(3) Oxidation number of oxygen decreases as well as increase

(4) Oxidation number of oxygen neither decreases nor increases
options: (1) Oxidation number of oxygen only decreases
(2) Oxidation number of oxygen only increases
(3) Oxidation number of oxygen decreases as well as increase
(4) Oxidation number of oxygen neither decreases nor increases

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Incorrect identification of oxidation states.
  • Failure to track electron transfer properly.
  • Confusing types of redox reaction.
  • Confusing roles of oxidants and reductants.
Note:

One can accurately solve redox reactions by avoiding these common mistakes and following a systematic approach to balancing redox reactions, understanding oxidation states, and carefully analyzing the roles of reductants and oxidants.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Balancing of Redox Reactions :-

• Ion-Electron method
    • Oxidation number change method

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question:
Balance the following reaction by ion-electron method in acidic medium :

Cr2O72- + C2O42- → Cr3+ + CO2
blocks.answer:
Separate the two half reactions and Balance Atoms other than H and O

Cr2O72- → 2Cr3+

C2O42- → 2CO2

Balance O-atoms by adding H2O and Balance H-atoms by the addition of H+

Cr2O72- + 14H+ → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O

C2O42- → 2CO2

Balance the charges by adding electrons

Cr2O72- + 14H+ + 6e- → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O      …………(1)

C2O42- → 2CO2 + 2e-                                          …………(2)

Multiply (2) equation by 3 and add to (1) to give

Cr2O72- + 14H+ + 6e- → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O

3C2O42- → 6CO2 + 6e-

—---------------------------------------------------------------

Cr2O72- + 3C2O42- + 14H+ → 2Cr3+ + 6CO2 + 7H2O

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.question:
Balance the following reaction by the oxidation number method :

MnO4- + Fe2+ → Mn2+ +  Fe3+
blocks.answer:
Write the oxidation number of all the atoms and change in oxidation number has occured in Mn and Fe.

MnO4-  →  Mn2+     …..(1)  (Decrement in oxidation no. by 5)

(+7)            (+2)

Fe2+ → Fe3+             …..(2)  (Increment in oxidation no. by 1)

(+2)      (+3)

To make increase and decrease equal, eq. (2) is multiplied by 5 and To balance oxygen, 4H2O are added to R.H.S. and to balance hydrogen, 8H+ are added to L.H.S.

MnO4- + 5Fe2++ 8H+ → Mn2+ +  5Fe3+ + 4H2O

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Equivalent Weight of Compounds

The equivalent weight of an oxidising agent or reducing agent is that weight which accepts or loses one mole electrons in a chemical reaction.

Normality

Normality of solution is defined as the number of equivalent of solute present in one liter (1000mL) solutions.

Formulas and Mathematical Relations

  • $\text{Equivalent weight (E)} = \frac{\text{Molecular weight}}{\text{No. of electrons gained/lost by one mole}}$
In Redox Change for oxidising agent or reducing agent n-factor is the change in oxidation number per mole of the substance.

  • $\text{Normality (N)} = \frac{\text{weight of solute (W)} \times 1000}{\text{equivalent weight of solute (E)} \times \text{V (ml) of solution}}$
Normality (N) = molarity(M) × Valence factor (n)

Law of Equivalence

For Redox Reactions :

Number of m. eq. of oxidant = Number of m. eq. of reductant

N1V1 = N2V2 is always true.

But (M1 × V1) × n1 = (M2 × V2) × n2 (always true where n term represents valency factor).

blocks.title: Some Oxidizing Agents/ Reducing Agents with Eq. Wt.
Example 1
blocks.question:
Find the number of moles of KMnO4 needed to oxidise one mole Cu2S in acidic medium. The reaction is-

KMnO4 + Cu2S  → Mn2+ + Cu2+ + SO2
blocks.answer:
From law of equivalence

equivalents of Cu2S = equivalents of KMnO4

moles of Cu2S × v.f = moles of KMnO4 × v.f.

1 × 8 = n2 × 5

n2 = $\frac{8}{5}$ = 1.6
